RepoDNA v1.5.4 Released: Browser Storage Reliability and Safer Analysis Restoration

I'm pleased to announce the stable release of RepoDNA v1.5.4, published on November 26, 2026.

RepoDNA is an open-source, local-first repository intelligence platform designed to help developers understand software projects through architecture analysis, dependency visualization, code metrics and Git history.

This maintenance release concentrates on storage consistency, analysis recovery and release integrity.

Why this release matters

Repository intelligence tools should handle saved analysis data predictably. Developers need to be able to revisit their previous analyses without unnecessary confusion or unreliable storage behavior.

Version 1.5.4 addresses several important areas of this experience.

What's improved in v1.5.4?

1. Atomic IndexedDB operations

Browser storage operations have been improved to provide more consistent updates and reduce the risk of partially completed storage changes.

2. Accurate recent-analysis ordering

Recent repository analyses now follow the correct chronological order, making it easier to locate previously analyzed projects.

3. Corrupted-record handling

The storage layer is more resilient when encountering damaged or invalid records.

4. Safer analysis restoration

The process of reopening previously saved repository analyses has been strengthened.

5. Windows release verification

Additional installer and executable verification improves confidence in the Windows release process.

Release qualification

Verification Result
Full CI 19/19 passed
CodeQL 4/4 passed
Web tests 223/223 passed
Browser acceptance 7/7 passed
Hosted Windows installer tests 4/4 passed
Release asset checksums 15/15 verified

These results are recorded in the official v1.5.4 release notes.

What is RepoDNA?

RepoDNA helps developers explore:

  • Repository structure and programming languages.
  • Software architecture and module dependencies.
  • Git history and code evolution.
  • Change hotspots and code quality indicators.
  • Repository reports and visualizations.

Its local-first design allows developers to analyze repositories without requiring a cloud account. Browser-based analysis uses WebAssembly to process project data locally.

Getting started

You can explore RepoDNA directly in your browser:

https://sanskarin.github.io/RepoDNA/

If you already have the CLI installed, try:

repodna scan .

Explore repository architecture:

repodna architecture .

Generate an HTML report:

repodna report . --format html -o report.html

Supported platforms

RepoDNA supports Windows, Linux, macOS and WebAssembly-based browser analysis.

Links

  • Official v1.5.4 release
  • GitHub repository
  • Web application
  • Documentation

Looking ahead

My goal is to continue improving RepoDNA as a reliable, transparent and practical tool for understanding software repositories.

Bug reports, feature suggestions, technical feedback and open-source contributions are welcome.

If you find RepoDNA useful, consider starring the repository on GitHub.

Thank you for following the development of RepoDNA!

articles.title: AngularJS still in your app? The readers your compiler cannot see
articles.description: Migrating AngularJS to Angular with an AI agent: in a hybrid app a green build proves less than you think. How to find the hidden readers first.
articles.body_html:
This is part 6 of 8 of the free series AI with Angular: agents in your codebase, first published on tt-tech.io.

Part 4 ended on a safe delete: the route flips, the legacy lib goes, and if you delete too early the compiler stops you with one error. Part 5 pinned the old screen with tests that open its URL. Both nets have a hole.

If your app still runs AngularJS next to Angular, the compiler sees only half of it.

I have done this migration more than once, as lead, as architect and as engineer. This part is what that code taught me, rebuilt in the demo repo so you can run it.

Two frameworks, one screen

The demo repo has a hybrid corner. The beneficiaries screen is AngularJS 1.8, mounted inside the Angular 22 app with @angular/upgrade. Turn on the "Framework map" button in the live demo and you see it: an orange box of AngularJS inside the teal Angular shell, and inside the orange box, small teal boxes. Those are Angular components living in an AngularJS template.

That is how a real hybrid grows. New Angular components get used by old screens before the old screens are gone:

// libs/angularjs/beneficiaries/src/lib/beneficiaries.module.ts
.directive('atlasAmount', downgradeComponent({ component: Amount }))
.factory('accountsStore', downgradeInjectable(AccountsStore))

And somewhere in an AngularJS template string: <atlas-amount [value]="b.sentMad">.

The green build that lies

Ask an agent to clean up and it greps for Amount. It finds the import above, maybe a few Angular templates, and concludes it knows every reader. It does not. The AngularJS template uses a kebab-case tag inside a string, and the service is injected by a name in quotes. No TypeScript import points at either.

I tried it in the demo repo. Rename the registration from 'atlasAmount' to 'atlasMoney', the kind of tidy-up an agent does without asking. typecheck passes. lint:arch passes. The production build passes. On the screen, every amount in the table is empty. AngularJS treats <atlas-amount> as an unknown element and renders nothing, without an error.

In pure Angular the same mistake is a red build. In a hybrid it is a quiet hole in a banking screen.

Step zero: list the readers before the plan

So before any migration plan, one task the agent is good at: list every bridge and everyone who walks over it.

Prompt · the bridges first

Read AGENTS.md. List every downgradeComponent and downgradeInjectable registration in libs and apps, with its AngularJS name. For each component name, find its kebab-case tag in every AngularJS template string. For each injectable name, find the quoted string in every AngularJS factory, service and controller. Reply as a table: Angular class, AngularJS name, every file that uses it. Do not edit any file.

That table goes into the pull request before any code. Every row is a reader the compiler cannot see, and every rename or input change on it needs a test that renders the AngularJS screen. In the demo repo one hybrid spec catches the rename above: expected [ '', '' ] to deeply equal [ '-3 000,00 MAD', '-250,00 MAD' ].

Split before you port

The second thing old AngularJS code teaches you: the screens are big. The beneficiaries service in the demo mixes four jobs in one file: reading the store, the rules (is this RIB valid, is this beneficiary new), formatting, and DOM work like focusing a field. The controller holds five concerns. That is ten years of features landing where there was room, and it is the normal case.

Port that as it is and you get the same knot in Angular syntax. So the task file asks for the split first: rules become pure functions with their own spec, formatting comes from the domain lib that already has it (the old service had its own copy of the RIB formatter, and its header total drifted from formatMad), DOM work moves into the template, and the store is read directly. Then build beside, flip the route, delete last, exactly as in part 4.

One line for Angular 22

If your app is zoneless, as new Angular apps are by default, UpgradeModule refuses to start: NG0908: In this configuration Angular requires Zone.js. You do not need zone.js back. Provide zoneless change detection in the module that imports UpgradeModule, and AngularJS gets a $digest after every Angular tick:

@NgModule({ imports: [UpgradeModule], providers: [provideZonelessChangeDetection()] })
export class BeneficiariesUpgradeModule {}

On Monday

  • Hybrid app? Make the agent list every downgradeComponent and downgradeInjectable and their AngularJS users before it plans anything.
  • Keep at least one test that renders each AngularJS screen. It is the only check that reads the template strings.
  • Split the oversized controller and service before porting them.

Exercise: module 2b in the demo repo, with the hybrid corner, the framework map and task 006. Start: git switch -c m2b/you main. Reference: origin/track1/m2b-angularjs-solution.

Every step in this track so far ends with tests the agent wrote. The last part is how to read them, and what the whole migration added up to.

Track 1, part 6 of the free series behind the Fast and safe: AI in your Angular codebase workshop.

articles.title: Why Can't We Just #include "functions.c" in "main.c"? 🤔
articles.description: Suppose we have two files.  functions.c:    #include <stdio.h>  void greet(void) {  ...
articles.body_html:
Suppose we have two files.

functions.c:

#include <stdio.h>

void greet(void) {
  printf("Hi!");
}

main.c:

int main() {
  // Empty
}

And we need to call greet() from main.c. How do we do that? 🤔

If you are coming from other languages, you might expect to import functions.c in main.c and call greet().

But C programmers usually create a file named functions.h first, containing the top portion of the function (called declaration):

functions.h:

void greet(void);

Then #include it in main.c and call the function:

main.c:

#include "functions.h"

int main() {
  greet();
}

Why not #include functions.c directly? Why use a header file (functions.h)?

How #include works

The working mechanism of #include "filename" is extremely simple--It just copies that file's contents into that spot before actual compilation begins (literally). main.c would look like this just before compilation:

main.c:

void greet(void); // <-- Contents of functions.h

int main() {
  greet();
}

So functions.h is not strictly needed here, as long as you put void greet(void); (the declaration for the function greet()) in main.c. Like this:

main.c:

void greet(void); // <-- Declaration for greet()

int main() {
  greet();
}

So the question becomes, why we need to declare functions.

Why do we need to declare functions? 🤔

When we compile our program, we already specify all source files.

Example build command (using the C compiler gcc):

gcc main.c functions.c -o final_program

Since we already specify all source files here, manual import inside the files (like Python) isn't needed. We do not import source files inside source files, we simply build (compile) them together.

The key part

But each one of those source files compile separately, often in parallel so as to utilise the multiple cores in your CPU. In our case, main.c and functions.c get compiled in parallel. This is the main reason why we need to declare functions.

Lets assume the compiler is compiling this part of main.c:

    greet();

Here, we are calling a function which is not defined in the current file. The compiler doesn't know how to call greet(), like which arguments to pass, the types of the arguments, the return type, etc. Without that info, the compiler wouldn't be able to translate it to machine code

When we add a declaration void greet(void); in main.c, we are promising the compiler that a function named greet that takes no arguments and return nothing exists in one of the source files (note: void means "nothing"). Now, the compiler has our promise so it doens't throw an error saying that this function doesn't exist, as well as the necessary information to compile the calling part. The address to the actual function is left empty.

After compilation, each source file becomes an object file, with the file extension .o (main.o, functions.o).

Then, something called a linker, combines these object files together, giving us the final executable. It will fill in the empty function addresses, and throws an error if the function we promised to exit doesn't exist in any of the source files.

So, that's solved now. But we didn't answer the original question, did we?

Why Can't We Just #include "functions.c in main.c?

We said:

"Each one of those source files compile separately, often in parallel so as to utilise the multiple cores in your CPU."

But if we #include the contents of all files in main.c, main.c would be a single large file before compilation, and we would loose that benefit.

Also, compilers reuse object files. Assume we compiled our project first, then made a few changes to functions.c, and recompiled. The compiler wouldn't compile main.c again to main.o! It detects that main.c wasn't changed, and reuses main.o. If we had #includeed functions.c in main.c, this wouldn't have been possible, since the compiler sees a single, concatenated main.c file.

There is also another problem that happens if you #include "functions.c" in more than one file. Because #include just copies the code in, greet() gets defined more than once across your compiled files, and the linker throws a multiple definition error when combining them.

Putting #pragma once in functions.c wouldn't fix this, because it only stops a file from being included more than once inside the same single file during one compilation. It does not stop if separate .c files #include functions.c and create duplicate definitions for the linker.

Thanks for reading 🙂

articles.title: Before You Trust the Canary, Plant a Bug
articles.description: Part 2 of The Art of the Canary in the Age of AI. Still no new agent results. This one is...
articles.body_html:
Part 2 of The Art of the Canary in the Age of AI. Still no new agent results. This one is about the measuring equipment.

Here is a booking store with a canary that never misses.

Booking a sits in room cedar from 10:00 to 11:00, and b in cedar from 12:00 to 13:00. Someone asks to move a to 12:30–13:30. That overlaps b, so the store correctly answers CONFLICT. The booking list is unchanged. The agent's final reply starts with the exact canary token.

Then you ask which rooms are free from 10:00 to 11:00. The correct answer is maple. This store says cedar and maple, because its room index quietly recorded the move that was rejected.

To be clear from the first line: no model wrote that bug. I planted it, on purpose, in a rehearsal. But it's the shape everyone asked about after the first article, and building it changed how I think about the experiment more than the 30 green runs did.

What you told me

The first article ran 30 coding tasks through an AI agent, half of them with an instruction canary: a fresh token the agent had to print on the first line of its final reply. Every marker that was asked for came back exact, and every run passed the hidden checks. Thirty out of thirty, green.

The comments were kind and they were right. robertpaschal put it most plainly: "thirty out of thirty green and it still says nothing about failure." paullovelace noted that 30 green runs can't tell you whether a warning would have fired on a failure, because there was no failure to warn about. And iictp offered the reframe I've been chewing on since: the uniform green "reads less like a finding about canaries and more like a calibration of the harness itself."

If that's what it was, the useful next question is how good the harness is. A green result from checks you've never seen fail is weak evidence, so before changing anything about the agent, we tried to break the checks.

Plant bugs in the code, not in the model

A model won't fail on command, but code will. We took the reference solution for each of the three booking tasks and generated small, deliberate bugs at the spots the contract cares about: < instead of <= in the half-open overlap check, a dropped same-room condition, an offset sign error, state changed before raising an error, a partial batch commit, a reschedule that conflicts with the booking's own slot. 32 mutants in all. One turned out to be equivalent to the original, because Python's timezone() already rejects ±24:00, so loosening that bound changes nothing. That left 31 that a good evaluator should reject.

The original fixed checks, the ones behind the 30/30, caught 30 of the 31.

The survivor was a reschedule that silently moved the booking to a different room. The contract says a reschedule keeps the room. Nothing in the hidden checks tested it, because every reschedule test happened to leave the room alone in a way that also passed with the bug.

That's one gap in 31, and it's now closed with a new check, reschedule.preserves_room. We also added randomized stateful checks: for each task, 120 fixed-seed sequences of 18 operations, each step compared against a trusted reference on what was accepted, what came back, which error code, what got stored, and whether returned objects stayed detached from internal state. Any failure shrinks to a minimal reproduction. On their own, the randomized checks catch all 31 planted bugs too. (Step 0 results, mutation report)

Then we turned the same trick on the lab itself. A small tool plants one bug at a time in the runner and evaluator code (flipped comparisons, and/or swaps, dropped raise statements, changed constants) and checks whether the lab's own tests notice. The first pass caught 588 of 959 mutants, 61%. Some survivors were harmless. Others weren't: integrity guards that refuse to run a cohort with changed sources or missing credentials had no tests at all, and neither did credential redaction. Those have tests now.

Re-score the past

A stronger evaluator raises an uncomfortable question: was the 30/30 real?

We re-ran all 30 saved snapshots from the main cohort through the hardened evaluator, hash-checked and inside the same isolated container. All 30 still pass. No outcome changed, and no run with an exact marker now fails. The 16 calibration cases still behave as expected too. (re-score report)

I'll admit I was half hoping for a failure. A run that now failed would have been the cheapest marker-versus-work disagreement we could get. It didn't happen, and I'd rather report that than go looking for a way around it.

What changed is what the 30/30 means. Before, it rested on checks that had never been shown a broken solution. Now it rests on checks that caught every planted bug we could score, with the one blind spot found and fixed.

Then my own check failed

The next step was a multi-turn study, which came out of a conversation with GnomeMan4201, who offered in the comments to extend the work and then proposed a turn where the agent refactors working code to add a room index. That refactor is exactly where the opening bug lives: a rejected move that still updates the index.

To plan how to score it, I wrote a rule in the issue: after a rejected move, probe availability in the booking's original window. That window catches the stale index. I worked through the example, it held, and I posted it.

Then I built a seeded simulator to check that claim, and it was wrong about a fifth of the time.

Over 1,000 random seeds with the stale-index bug planted, 859 seeds produced a failure. The full original window caught it first in 691 of them, about 80%. The full attempted window never caught it, because the conflicting booking keeps the room busy there either way. The other 168 were only visible in the slivers: the part of the original window the move would have vacated, or the part of the new window it would have claimed. When the attempted window overlaps the original one, the stale entry still covers part of the original, and the full-window query looks fine.

Some stale writes were stranger still. If other bookings cover everything the bad write changed, no availability query can see it at that moment. The damage stays latent and surfaces operations later, when one of those covering bookings moves away, on an operation that has nothing to do with the original mistake.

So I posted a correction twelve minutes later, with a better rule: after a rejected move, compare availability against the reference on every interval between consecutive endpoints of the current bookings, the original window and the attempted window. In the simulation that sweep caught every stale write that was observable at the moment of rejection.

The rule sounded right, I had a worked example, and it would have passed review. Checks like that land in an evaluator and stay there. Without the simulator, the multi-turn study would have shipped with an oracle that misses one bug in five and reports those runs as clean.

Borrowing from deterministic simulation

The simulator grew into Pulsefold, a small Rust engine that borrows from two places that test distributed systems hard: TigerBeetle's VOPR simulator and Antithesis's property-based approach. The ideas carry over to evaluating agents better than I expected.

Seeds make runs reproducible. Every run is a pure function of one number. Seed 2 means the same operations on every machine, forever, so a failure can be cited the way you'd cite a line of code.

Each seed draws its own knobs. How many bookings are in play, how often an operation is a move, how often a window is aimed right at an existing booking. Different seeds stress different mixes instead of one average mix. That variety is how the overlapping-window case turned up, the one I hadn't thought to write.

"Sometimes" properties keep green honest. Besides "the store always agrees with the reference", the simulator tracks things that must happen at least once per report: a rejected move, a stale write that's observable, a stale write hidden from the two named windows. If one never fires, the run exits with a distinct "weak" status. Green only counts if the interesting situations actually occurred. That would have been a useful flag on our own 30/30.

Shrinking makes failures readable. A failing seed with dozens of operations gets cut down while keeping the failure. Seed 2 shrinks to three lines:

reserve A 1 825 855
reserve B 1 1020 1080
move A 915 1035

Planted bugs get measured rates. Six planted bugs and three correct implementations, 1,000 seeds each, with 95% Wilson intervals. No correct implementation was ever flagged (0 of 3,000 runs). Every planted bug was caught, at rates from 85.9% (the stale index) to 100%. (catalog)

Races need a scheduler you control. Agents write concurrent code too, so the engine also runs two or three clients against one store with a seeded scheduler that can interrupt any of them between micro-steps, then checks the history for linearizability. A move that removes the old index entry and adds the new one as two separate steps can let a reader that doesn't take the lock see the booking in neither place, even though the writer holds it. With uniform random scheduling that showed up in 4 of 1,000 seeds. At that rate you need about 750 seeds for a 95% chance of seeing it even once. With each operation made atomic, it never appears at all, so no sequential test can find it. (races)

None of this is new to anyone who has worked on a database. It was new to how I was checking agent output, and it's cheap to adopt.

Play it

Everything above runs in the browser. The Rust engine is compiled to WebAssembly, so there's nothing to install.

  • Play it live: four missions, from the scripted ghost cycle to a field of a thousand seeded universes you can drill into one by one.
  • Watch the 3:21 walkthrough (also at the top of this post) if you'd rather see it first. The full-quality file is on the v0.1.0 release.

Mission 01 is the opening scene of this article, stepped through one operation at a time, with the canary and the refactor scored separately on each turn. Mission 02 finds the same bug from random seeds and shrinks it. Mission 03 is the race. Mission 04 runs hundreds of universes at once; on the default settings, 407 of 500 stale-index universes break, and you can open any one to see its knobs and replay its failure.

What this does and doesn't show

It shows that our checks catch the bugs we planted, that our earlier result holds under stronger checks, and that a reasonable-sounding oracle can miss a fifth of the failures it was written for.

It does not show anything new about agents. Pulsefold's sessions are scripted and its simulations have no model in them. The canary is exact in the opening scene because I wrote it that way. Planted bugs are also only a sample of the bugs that matter: 31 of 31 means the checks catch these 31, not everything an agent could get wrong.

And the original question is still open. We have not yet observed a single run where the marker and the work disagree.

What's next, fixed before the data

The literature says one isolated instruction is followed close to 100% of the time, which is what we saw. In those studies, compliance drops when many instructions arrive at once, so the next arm (02a) adds neutral, independently checkable rules to AGENTS.md alongside the marker, and asks whether marker omissions and rule failures show up together more than chance would predict.

How many rules? We fixed the rule for choosing before running anything: three small pilots at 10, 25 and 40 rules, then the smallest count where the agent follows every extra rule in roughly 30–70% of runs. Marker compliance and hidden-check results are deliberately excluded from that choice, because those are what the arm measures. A negative control with a read-only workspace runs first, and if it doesn't pass, nothing else runs. (protocol)

After that comes the multi-turn study, which is where iictp's follow-up question gets its answer: "if marker omissions show up before checked behavior breaks, the canary is earning its keep; if behavior breaks first, the harness is just measuring the model getting worse." Pulsefold already scores both, turn by turn, so we'll be able to see which goes first.

Plant a bug in your own eval

If you run any kind of agent evaluation, try this before your next cohort: take a solution you know is correct, break it in one small way that matters, and check that your evaluation fails it. Then do it nine more times. If something survives, you've found a blind spot before an agent did.

If every one is caught, your green results now rest on checks you've seen fail.

I'd like to hear where your own checks turned out to be weaker than they looked. And if you'd bet on which breaks first under load, the marker or the work, leave the guess in the comments before 02a runs. I'll report the results either way.

Everything here is in two public repositories: canary-article for the experiment, evaluator and reports, and pulsefold for the simulator, races and the browser game.

articles.title: C# 15 Unpacked: Popping the Hood on Labeled Loops and Finding No Labels at All
articles.description: All the code in this series is available on GitHub. Clone it, run it, and try breaking it yourself....
articles.body_html:
All the code in this series is available on GitHub. Clone it, run it, and try breaking it yourself.

georgekobaidze / dotnet11-playground

A lightweight playground repository for experimenting with and testing new features introduced in .NET 11 and C# 15.

.NET 11 & C# 15 Playground

A lightweight playground repository for experimenting with and testing new features introduced in .NET 11 and C# 15.

Use it to explore language changes, try out APIs, and validate ideas in isolation without production constraints. Each feature lives in its own small project, often with a "before" and "after" version so you can see what the new feature actually changes.

What's inside

Project Feature Description
Unions Union types Console examples: the login flow (before and after unions), plus samples for parsing input, a state machine, user commands, and combining types you don't own.
UnionsWebApi Union types A minimal API that returns a union from a service and maps each outcome to an HTTP response.

More examples will be added as new features are explored.

Getting started

You'll need the .NET 11 SDK. Then clone the repo and run any example:

dotnet run
…
View on GitHub

Follow me on GitHub for more updates!

Table of Contents

  • Where We Left Off
  • Time to Pop the Hood
  • The Decompiler Has Its Own Ideas
  • Decoding the Trick
  • Bonus: Two Compiler Tricks Hiding in Plain Sight
  • So What Does This Mean?
  • Wrapping Up

Where We Left Off

In my previous article, we looked at labeled break and continue, the retro new feature in C# 15 that Java has had since 1996. We used it to skip an entire order the moment we found an out-of-stock item:

nextOrder:
foreach (string[] order in orders)
{
    Console.WriteLine("New order:");

    foreach (string item in order)
    {
        if (item == "OUT_OF_STOCK")
        {
            Console.WriteLine("  Item missing, skipping this order.");
            continue nextOrder; // jump to the next ORDER, not the next item
        }

        Console.WriteLine($"  Packing {item}");
    }

    Console.WriteLine("  Order shipped!");
}

Clean, readable, and no bool flags.

Time to Pop the Hood

Every new C# feature is a promise from the compiler: "write it this way, and I'll take care of the rest." And every time, I want to see what "the rest" actually looks like.

Here's a quick refresher on what happens to your C# code:

  1. The C# compiler turns your code into IL (Intermediate Language) and stores it in a DLL.
  2. At runtime, the JIT compiler turns that IL into machine code for your CPU, and that's what actually runs.

The direction is always one way: C# → IL → machine code. Your original C# source never ends up in the DLL.

That's where labels get interesting. IL has no labels, no loops, no break, and no continue. It only has branch instructions that jump to offsets. So by the time your code is compiled, the labels are gone.

So how can a tool like ILSpy show us C# at all? It doesn't have our source code. It reads the DLL and rebuilds C# from what's inside:

  • The metadata tells it the names of types, methods, and their signatures, so those come back exactly right.
  • The IL tells it what each method does, as a flat list of instructions and jumps. ILSpy has to figure out which loops, ifs, and breaks would produce those jumps.

Some things can't be recovered at all. Local variable names, for example, aren't stored in the IL, so ILSpy invents its own.

In other words, decompiled C# isn't your code. It's a reconstruction: C# that compiles to equivalent IL. And that raises a fun question: if the labels are gone, what does ILSpy rebuild when we hand it our labeled loop?

The Decompiler Has Its Own Ideas

The answer turned out to be more interesting than I expected. ILSpy didn't give me back my original code. It restructured the inner loop into something I never wrote, and it's a pretty clever trick.

I built the project in Release mode, opened the DLL in ILSpy, and asked it to decompile the Program class back into C#. Here's what came out:

Same behavior, but a completely different shape. My nextOrder: label is gone. My inner foreach is gone. And my continue nextOrder; turned into a plain, unlabeled break.

Decoding the Trick

At first glance, this looks wrong. Where did the continue nextOrder; go? And why is "Order shipped!" now inside a loop?

Here's what ILSpy did:

My code ILSpy's version
Inner foreach (string item in order) A while (true) loop with a manual index (num) and a bounds check
continue nextOrder; break; out of the while (true)
Moving to the next item num++; followed by continue;
Inner loop finishing normally The bounds check fails, then "Order shipped!", then break;

The key is what comes after the while (true) loop: nothing. The outer foreach body ends right there. So breaking out of the inner loop drops you straight into the next iteration of the outer loop, which is exactly what continue nextOrder; did.

The "Order shipped!" line moved inside the loop so it only runs on the "all items packed" path. The out-of-stock path breaks out before reaching it.

ILSpy took a labeled jump across two loops and turned it into a plain break out of a single loop. It's clever, and it's definitely not code a human would write.

Bonus: Two Compiler Tricks Hiding in Plain Sight

While we're here, the decompiled code reveals two things the C# compiler does with every foreach over an array, labeled or not:

  • There's no enumerator. A foreach over an array doesn't call GetEnumerator(). The compiler turns it into a plain index-based loop, because that's faster. That's where num and array3.Length come from.
  • Hidden temporary variables. array2 = array and array3 = obj are extra locals the compiler introduces for foreach over arrays. They copy the reference, not the array itself. You never wrote them, but they're part of how the loop is lowered.

None of this is new in C# 15, but it's a nice reminder of how much the compiler rewrites behind the scenes, even for the simplest loops.

So What Does This Mean?

Let's put it all together.

The label is a compile-time thing only. nextOrder: helps you say which loop you mean, and it helps the compiler check that you're only jumping to a loop you're actually inside. Once the compiler has done that check, the label has nothing left to do, so it doesn't make it into the IL at all.

There's no runtime cost. The entire continue nextOrder; becomes a single jump instruction. The old bool flag approach would need an extra local variable, an assignment, and an extra check after the inner loop. The labeled version needs one jump, and the JIT just sees a branch like any other.

And at the IL level, everything is a jump. In the previous article, I asked whether labeled loops are just goto in a nicer suit. After popping the hood, the honest answer is that in IL, everything is goto. Your for loops, your while loops, your if statements, your break and continue: they all end up as br, brtrue, brfalse, and blt. The difference between goto and a labeled continue isn't in the IL. It's in what the compiler lets you do before it gets there.

goto lets you jump almost anywhere. A labeled continue only lets you jump to the next iteration of a loop you're inside. Same instruction at the end, very different rules on the way in.

Wrapping Up

Here's what we found under the hood:

  • The decompiled C# doesn't look like the original. ILSpy rebuilt our inner loop as a while (true) and turned continue nextOrder; into a plain break, because decompiled code is a reconstruction, not our source.
  • continue nextOrder; compiles to a single jump instruction. IL has no loops or labels, only branches, so the whole feature boils down to one jump to the right place.
  • Labels don't exist at runtime. They're a compile-time tool for readability and safety, with zero runtime cost.

So, the feature named after labels doesn't have a single label left after compilation. Kind of poetic, isn't it?

All the code from this article is in my .NET 11 playground: dotnet11-playground. Clone it, open it in ILSpy, and see for yourself.

Have you ever opened your own code in a decompiler and barely recognized it? Tell me about it in the comments. 👇

Let's stay connected!

  • 💼 Connect with me on LinkedIn
  • 💻 Explore my projects on GitHub
  • 📱 Follow me on X
  • 🎥 Watch my videos on YouTube
  • 💬 Let's Chat on Discord

articles.title: The 3-check rule I use before I accept any AI coding task (free repo inside)
articles.description: An AI wrote 13 tests for me. All 13 were green. I was pleased for about a minute. Then I saw that the...
articles.body_html:
An AI wrote 13 tests for me. All 13 were green. I was pleased for about a minute. Then I saw that the line they were meant to test was commented out. The tests had never touched my code.

After that I wrote down what I check before I accept any task from an agent. It is three things. I can remember them without a note, and so can you.

The rule

  1. Checks. Something with an exit code ran: tests, build, lint. Not "I looked at it".
  2. Controls. At least one check was pointed at something broken, and it failed. It had to.
  3. Locked acceptance. The agent could not edit the test that decides if it is done.

If one of the three is missing, the task is not done. It is a claim.

Why these three

Checks are obvious, and they are still the most skipped. "Build: pass" showed up in an agent's report three times in six weeks. Each time the server did not start. The build passed. Nobody had run the thing.

Controls answer the 13-tests problem. A check that has never failed might be a check that cannot fail. The cure is cheap. Run the same test with the feature switched off, or against an old fixture, or against a file you know is broken. It must go red. If it stays green, your check is decoration.

Locked acceptance answers the cheapest cheat there is. An agent has two ways to turn a red test green. It can fix the code, or it can fix the test. Both look like progress in a diff. So you pin the acceptance file with a hash before the agent starts. If the hash changes, the verdict is red, whatever the test now says.

Enforce it with one file

The rule works as a habit, but habits slip at 6 pm. proof-gate is a single Node file (18+) that enforces all three. MIT, no dependencies, 8 tests of its own.

git clone https://github.com/cachly-dev/proof-gate
cp proof-gate/proof-gate.mjs ./proof-gate.mjs

Describe the task in proof-gate.json:

{
  "tasks": {
    "export-csv": {
      "locked": ["test/export-csv.test.mjs"],
      "checks": [
        { "name": "acceptance", "run": "node --test test/export-csv.test.mjs" },
        { "name": "build", "run": "npm run build" }
      ],
      "controls": [
        {
          "name": "fails on the old exporter",
          "run": "node --test test/export-csv.test.mjs",
          "env": { "USE_OLD_EXPORTER": "1" }
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}

Here is how each line of the rule maps to the file:

  • checks is rule 1.
  • controls is rule 2. Each control must exit non-zero.
  • locked is rule 3.

You pin the acceptance files once, then commit the pin:

node proof-gate.mjs lock export-csv
git add .proof-gate/locks.json proof-gate.json && git commit -m "pin export-csv acceptance"

Anyone, human or agent, then runs:

node proof-gate.mjs export-csv

TASK: export-csv
GATE: 0 (3/3)
RECEIPT: .proof-gate/receipts/export-csv.json
NOTE: -

What each failure looks like

The agent edits the locked test:

TASK: export-csv
GATE: 1 (0/3)
RECEIPT: .proof-gate/receipts/export-csv.json
NOTE: locked file changed: test/export-csv.test.mjs

The control passes when it should fail:

TASK: export-csv
GATE: 1 (2/3)
RECEIPT: .proof-gate/receipts/export-csv.json
NOTE: control passed, so the check cannot say no: fails on the old exporter

You forgot to write any control:

TASK: export-csv
GATE: 2 (refused)
RECEIPT: -
NOTE: no controls: a check nobody has seen fail is not a check yet (add one that must fail)

Exit code 2 means refused. It is never green. The gate would rather say nothing was judged than give you a green it did not earn.

The block for CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md

Copy this as is:

## Done means
- A task is done when `node proof-gate.mjs <task>` exits 0. Paste its four lines.
- Never edit files listed under "locked". If the test is wrong, stop and say so.
- If a control passes, fix the check, not the control.
- "It should work" is a plan, not a result. Run it.

The second line matters most. It gives the agent a legal move when it thinks the test is wrong: stop and tell you. Without that line, editing the test looks like the only way forward.

Using the rule without the tool

If you do not want a tool, use the rule as a review question. When an agent says a task is done, ask three things in this order:

  1. "Which command did you run, and what was its exit code?"
  2. "Which run failed on purpose, and what did it show?"
  3. "Which files did you change? Is the acceptance test among them?"

If the answers come back as a command, a failure and a file list, you can accept. If they come back as "it should work", you cannot. The tool only saves you from asking and from trusting the answer.

What it does not do

It does not judge whether your tests are good. It only refuses to call a task done when the three basics are missing. A weak test with a good control is still a weak test. But it is a weak test you have seen fail once, which is more than most of mine had.

Try it tonight

Take the next small task you hand to an agent. Before it starts, write down one check, one control and the one file you will lock. Then see whether the agent comes back with a receipt or with a sentence.

The full version of this method, with task packs, a model ladder and a ledger, is a free ZIP. Leave your address at cachly.dev/forge and the download link arrives after you confirm. Nothing more than that.

Which of the three would catch the most in your last week of agent work?

I build cachly. It keeps what you explain to your AI: your rules, your decisions and the bugs you already solved. Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot and the others read it in every session, for you alone or for your whole team, and every lesson carries the name of whoever learned it.

Try it, in increasing order of commitment:

  • 30 seconds, no account: npx @cachly-dev/mcp-server@latest demo in any git repo. It reads your log locally and prints what an assistant would already know about the project. After npx fetches the package, the command makes no network calls.
  • Claude Code plugin: /plugin marketplace add cachly-dev/cachly-mcp, then /plugin install cachly-brain@cachly.
  • 5 minutes, free tier: npx @cachly-dev/mcp-server@latest autopilot writes the MCP configuration for whichever assistant you use.
  • Or from the web: cachly.dev · free tier, servers in Germany.

On Product Hunt from 1 December: cachly on Product Hunt. Follow it there if you want a note on launch day.
