articles.title: Move your custom video player into Document Picture-in-Picture (controls included)
articles.description: TL;DR   video.requestPictureInPicture() only takes the <video>, so your custom...
articles.body_html:
TL;DR

video.requestPictureInPicture() only takes the <video>, so your custom controls vanish. documentPictureInPicture.requestWindow() opens an always-on-top window you fill with your own DOM. We'll move a live player (hls.js included) into it without interrupting playback, copy styles, fix keyboard shortcuts, move it back on close, and fall back to classic PiP where Document PiP doesn't exist. Tested in Chromium 158 with hls.js 1.7.4.

Browser support (Nov 2026)

Browser Document PiP Notes
Chrome / Edge desktop ✅ 116+ disallowReturnToOpener 124+, preferInitialWindowPlacement 130+
Firefox desktop ✅ 151+ shipped May 2026
Safari ❌ use classic requestPictureInPicture()
Chrome Android ❌ use classic API

Sources: Chrome for Developers, Firefox 151 release notes.

1. The starting player 🎥

A normal custom player: one container, a video, a control bar.

<!-- index.html -->
<button id="pipBtn">Pop out</button>
<div id="slot">
  <div class="player" id="player">
    <video id="v" muted playsinline></video>
    <div class="controls">
      <button class="play">Pause</button>
      <button class="fs">Fullscreen</button>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/hls.js@1.7.4/dist/hls.min.js"></script>
<script type="module" src="./player.js"></script>

/* player.css */
.player { position: relative; width: 640px; }
.controls { background: rgb(20, 20, 20); color: white; }

2. Open the window and move the player

The whole trick is append(). You're not cloning anything; the same node moves to the new document.

// pip.js
export async function openDocPip(player) {
  const pip = await documentPictureInPicture.requestWindow({ width: 640, height: 400 });
  copyStyles(pip);                       // step 3
  pip.document.body.append(player);      // move, don't clone
  pip.addEventListener('pagehide', () => {
    document.getElementById('slot').append(player);   // move it home on close
  });
  return pip;
}

Does playback survive the move? I ran the finished demo from this post (all of steps 2 to 6, fMP4 HLS through hls.js) in Chromium 158 with a Playwright script that logs currentTime, presses k inside the PiP window, closes it, then presses k in the page:

$ node test-move.js
before         1.22 paused=false
in pip         1.81 paused=false inPipDoc= true
controls bg    rgb(20, 20, 20)
fs button      none
after k in pip 1.83 paused=true
after k again  2.83 paused=false
back home      3.34 paused=false inMain= true
k in main doc  3.35 paused=true

No reset and no pause when moving in either direction; the hls.js instance kept feeding the same element after it changed documents. (I also ran the move with a plain progressive MP4: same result.) The keyboard lines only work because of step 4.

⚠️ Note: requestWindow() must be called from a user gesture (a click handler), or the promise rejects. You can't open it automatically on scroll.

3. Copy your styles

The PiP document starts empty. Before copying, my .controls background computed to rgba(0, 0, 0, 0); after, rgb(20, 20, 20). This is the pattern from Chrome's docs:

// pip.js
function copyStyles(pip) {
  for (const sheet of document.styleSheets) {
    try {
      const css = [...sheet.cssRules].map(r => r.cssText).join('');
      const style = document.createElement('style');
      style.textContent = css;
      pip.document.head.append(style);
    } catch {
      // cross-origin sheet: cssRules throws, so link it instead
      const link = document.createElement('link');
      link.rel = 'stylesheet';
      link.href = sheet.href;
      pip.document.head.append(link);
    }
  }
}

💡 Tip: if you use CSS-in-JS that injects styles at runtime, styles added after you open the window won't be copied. Open the window after your player has rendered once.

4. Stop reaching for document 🛠️

This is where most players break. After the move:

document.querySelector('.play');         // null: the button is in the other document
document.addEventListener('keydown', f); // never fires while the PiP window has focus

I confirmed both: a key pressed in the PiP window reached a listener on pip.document and not one on the page's document. Click handlers bound directly on buttons kept working, since the nodes carry their listeners.

Refactor the player to resolve everything from its own root:

// player.js
export function mountPlayer(root) {
  const video = root.querySelector('video');
  const playBtn = root.querySelector('.play');
  playBtn.onclick = () => (video.paused ? video.play() : video.pause());

  const onKey = (e) => {
    if (e.key === 'k' || e.key === ' ') { e.preventDefault(); playBtn.click(); }
  };
  let keyDoc = null;
  function bindKeys() {
    keyDoc?.removeEventListener('keydown', onKey);
    keyDoc = root.ownerDocument;          // whichever document the player is in now
    keyDoc.addEventListener('keydown', onKey);
  }
  bindKeys();
  return { video, rebind: bindKeys };
}

Call rebind() after every move:

// main.js
import { mountPlayer } from './player.js';
import { openDocPip } from './pip.js';

const root = document.getElementById('player');
const player = mountPlayer(root);
const hls = new Hls();
hls.loadSource('/hls_long/index.m3u8');
hls.attachMedia(player.video);

document.getElementById('pipBtn').onclick = async () => {
  if ('documentPictureInPicture' in window) {
    const pip = await openDocPip(root);
    player.rebind();
    root.classList.add('in-pip');
    pip.addEventListener('pagehide', () => {
      root.classList.remove('in-pip');
      queueMicrotask(player.rebind);
    });
  } else if (document.pictureInPictureEnabled) {
    await player.video.requestPictureInPicture();   // classic fallback: video only
  }
};

5. Watch out for cross-window instanceof

The PiP window has its own globals. From my test:

v instanceof HTMLVideoElement                                   // true (node created in the page)
pip.document.createElement('div') instanceof HTMLDivElement     // false
pip.document.createElement('div') instanceof pip.HTMLDivElement // true

If your player or UI library creates nodes inside the PiP document and type-checks them, use el.nodeName === 'DIV' or el.ownerDocument.defaultView.HTMLDivElement.

6. Hide what doesn't work in PiP

pip.document.fullscreenEnabled was false in my run, so a fullscreen button is dead weight. Chrome documents a media query for this (Chrome 123+):

/* player.css */
@media all and (display-mode: picture-in-picture) {
  .fs { display: none; }
}
/* backup that doesn't depend on the media query */
.player.in-pip .fs { display: none; }

⚠️ Note: in headless Chromium the display-mode: picture-in-picture query did not match inside the PiP window, which is why the .in-pip class is there. Check the media query in a real headed browser before relying on it alone.

7. Close the window from your code

The viewer isn't the only one who should close the window. Two cases I'd handle from day one:

  • The video ends. A floating window showing a finished video is clutter.
  • Your SPA unmounts the player. If a route change destroys the player component while it's floating, you're left with an always-on-top window holding a dead element (and, with hls.js, possibly a leaked instance).

documentPictureInPicture.window returns the open window or null, so closing is one line. Closing fires the same pagehide handler from step 2, which moves the player home:

// main.js (continued)
// window.* so this doesn't throw a ReferenceError in Safari, where the API doesn't exist
const closeDocPip = () => window.documentPictureInPicture?.window?.close();

player.video.addEventListener('ended', closeDocPip);

// in your framework's unmount / cleanup hook:
export function destroyPlayer() {
  closeDocPip();
  hls.destroy();
}

Checked in the same Chromium run: after seeking to half a second before the end, the window closed on ended and the player was back in #slot:

$ node test-close.js
open?         true
after ended   { open: false, playerHome: true }

Rules the API enforces

  • One PiP window per tab. A second requestWindow() closes the first.
  • The window can't be navigated, and the site can't set its position.
  • It closes when the opener tab closes.
  • width and height go together; pass both or neither.
  • Optional: disallowReturnToOpener: true (Chrome 124+) hides the back-to-tab button; preferInitialWindowPlacement: true (Chrome 130+) opens at the default spot instead of the viewer's last one.

Things to know

  • Tested: headless Chromium 158.0.8127.36 via Playwright, hls.js 1.7.4, progressive MP4 and fMP4 HLS.
  • Not tested: Firefox (support is from Mozilla's release notes), Safari fallback on a real device, and window sizing. Headless ignored my requested size and didn't enforce the user-gesture rule, so those behaviors come from the docs.

What's next

  • Put captions and a chapter list in the PiP window. That's where Document PiP beats the classic API for course and long-form content.
  • For live streams, try moving a chat panel in alongside the video. Same pattern, more DOM.

articles.title: Scoring "rare" answers in a daily trivia game with a softmax over Wikipedia signals
articles.description: I run a daily football trivia game where the goal is not just a right answer but a rare one. "Name a...
articles.body_html:
I run a daily football trivia game where the goal is not just a right answer but a rare one. "Name a Chelsea player": the first names everyone thinks of are right but worth 10 points. A name hardly anyone else would think of is worth 100.

So the whole game depends on one number per answer: how likely is a player to name him? Here is how that number is built, and the mistakes along the way.

First version: count real answers

The obvious approach is to score each name by how often people actually type it. It falls apart on day one. With a few dozen answers per question, one person naming an obscure player pushes him ahead of legends nobody happened to type yet.

I needed a prior: a guess at how famous each player is before anyone answers.

A softmax over public signals

For each question, every right answer gets a probability:

p_i = exp(w · x_i) / Σ_j exp(w · x_j)

The features x_i all come from public Wikipedia and Wikidata data:

  • page views of the player's article (log)
  • how many language editions have an article about him (log)
  • years with the team in question (log)
  • clicks from the team's article to the player's, from the Wikimedia clickstream dump (log)
  • whether he played there in the last five seasons

The weights w are fitted by maximum likelihood on real answers. On the first fit, standardised, page views came out at 1.12, language editions 0.98, years with the team 0.36, clickstream 0.16 and recent seasons 0.16. Fame beats tenure by a lot.

Real answers then blend in on top, with a strong prior (K = 300). With K = 30, the old bug came back.

A guard for the obvious names

The model alone still let some household names score high on some questions. So there is a hard rule: a question's most familiar answers by the model never score above the second tier (top 5%) or the third (top 12%). A hand-picked list of 20 obvious names across 9 popular questions is a test case: none of them may ever reach 75 points.

Did it work?

Backtest on 448 real answers to 142 questions. Each answer is scored only from the other answers to its question, and the model is fitted on four fifths of the questions and tested on the rest. The target share per tier is 25 / 25 / 20 / 18 / 12.

Distance from target (L1) Obvious names at 75+ (of 180)
Before: rough estimate, K = 30, no guard 36.0 96
After: model, K = 300, guard 24.8 0

The cost shows up in the second-rarest tier: it gets 5.6% of answers instead of 18%. Most people name familiar players, and the guard keeps those down. Loosening it would fill that tier, but it would also let a name like Ivanović (Chelsea, ranked 134 of 1,193 by the model) score 75. I'd rather the rare tier feel earned.

Refitting every night, carefully

A Cloudflare Worker cron refits the weights at 23:30 UTC on every answer so far, warm-started from the current weights, and stores the result for the next day. The new fit is thrown away, and yesterday's kept, if:

  • there are fewer than 200 answers,
  • it does more than 3 points worse on a fixed fifth of the questions, or
  • any of the obvious names would score 75+.

It takes about half a second of CPU at 455 answers. A synthetic run at 20,000 answers takes about 2.5 s.

Same answer, same day, same score

The last rule came from players, not data: if two people name the same player on the same day, they must get the same points. So the first request for a question each day freezes its score table from answers up to the day before. Today's answers only count from tomorrow.

The game is at footballkrillion.org if you want to see how rare your answers are.

articles.title: Drawing voxel pets on a plain 2D canvas (no WebGL, no three.js)
articles.description: I wanted chunky, cute voxel pets for a focus timer, and I wanted them to stay smooth on a cheap...
articles.body_html:
I wanted chunky, cute voxel pets for a focus timer, and I wanted them to stay smooth on a cheap Android phone. So instead of WebGL or a 3D library, the pets are drawn by a tiny ray caster that writes pixels into an ordinary 2D canvas. The whole engine is about 350 lines.

Here's how it works, and what I learned. (The app is Voxipaw: your pet grows up a little with every minute you focus. Everything below is running there.)

1. A pet is a list of boxes

Every pet is just an array of oriented boxes: body, head, snout, ears, four legs, tail. Each box has a centre, half-sizes, an optional rotation matrix, a colour family (fur, belly, ear…) and a part id.

function block(c, size, fam, part, opts = {}) {
  return { c, h: { x: size.x / 2, y: size.y / 2, z: size.z / 2 }, fam, part, ...opts };
}

Animation never touches pixels. A pose is a handful of numbers (tail wag, head turn, leg swing, ear angle), and each frame we rebuild the box list by rotating parts around pivot points: legs around the hip, the tail around its base, ears around the top of the head.

2. Each pixel shoots a ray

The camera is a true isometric one (yaw 45°, pitch 30°), so it's orthographic: every ray is parallel. For each pixel in the sprite's bounding box we start a ray far in front of the pet and test it against every box.

The ray-box test happens in the box's own frame (multiply by the inverse rotation), which turns it into the classic axis-aligned slab test. It returns the distance, which axis was hit (x, y or z) and the sign. That's the face.

// nearest box wins
for (const b of blocks) {
  const hit = hitBlock(origin, dir, b);
  if (hit && hit.t < depth[i]) { depth[i] = hit.t; id[i] = b.part; col[i] = shadeOf(b, hit); }
}

It sounds slow, and per pixel it is, but the sprites are small and a pet is only a few dozen boxes, so it's fast enough to animate smoothly in plain JavaScript.

3. Shading with four tones, not lighting maths

Real lighting looks muddy at this size. Instead, every colour family has a ramp of four hand-picked shades, and the face normal picks one:

const lam = dot(normal, LIGHT);
const tone = normal.y > 0.6 ? 0 : lam > 0.4 ? 1 : lam > 0.18 ? 2 : 3;

Tops are always the brightest tone, faces towards the light the next, and so on. That's the whole "voxel art" look: flat, crisp, readable.

4. Outlines for free

Because we kept a part id for every pixel, outlines are a second pass: if a pixel's neighbour belongs to a different part (or is empty), darken it. You get the dark edge around the silhouette and the soft lines between head and body, with no geometry work.

Faces (eyes, nose, a little mouth when it barks) are painted by a per-face callback: a box can say "on my x+ face, at these local coordinates, paint eye".

5. Growing up is just proportions

The pet grows from a tiny puppy to a grown dog over about 50 hours of focus. There is only one rig. Age is a number from 0 to 1, and it changes proportions:

  • head size shrinks relative to the body,
  • legs and body get longer,
  • the snout gets longer, ears less floppy.

So the same box list, with different sizes, covers every age. No new art per stage.

6. Keeping it smooth on cheap phones

  • Ray-cast only what moves. The home's scenery and items (kennel, trees, toys) are ray-cast once and cached as images; only the pet is re-rendered as it moves.
  • Draw the pet at 1×, scale with imageSmoothingEnabled = false. The canvas does the upscaling for free and it stays crisp.
  • A "lite" mode. If the frame time stays above ~22 ms, the app re-renders the pet less often and works out the water light only 20 times a second. It tries normal mode again later, so one slow moment doesn't stick.

What I'd do differently

  • I started with AI-generated illustrations cut into a 2D rig. It never looked right when the pet moved. Going fully voxel and drawing everything from boxes fixed that, and it made the art far easier to change.
  • The pet is still ray-cast fresh for each pose. Caching recent poses would save more battery on slow phones, and it's next on my list.

Try it

The app is free in the browser, no account: voxipaw.kionesis.com. Pick an animal, start a timer, and watch it nap. If you're curious how a specific part works (the water, the walking, the home growing), ask in the comments.

Transparency note: Voxipaw was built with the help of an AI coding assistant, and this post was drafted with AI help too. The pets and art are drawn by the code, not by image AI.

articles.title: A CSV cleaner that refuses to guess: two bugs that silently corrupted money
articles.description: European decimal commas that multiply amounts by 100, and 'normalised' dates like 2026-13-13. Both caught by one invariant: cleaning must not change the sum of the amount column.
articles.body_html:
Last night I built a free CSV cleaner
that runs entirely in the browser. Not because the world needs another CSV tool, but because
I sell a "send me your messy sheet, I'll clean it" service and the funnel was empty. A free
tool that actually works is the cheapest way to prove competence.

While writing it I hit two bugs that would have silently corrupted money. Both were caught by
tests, and both are worth stealing.

Bug 1: the decimal comma that multiplied amounts by 100

European files write 1200,00. US files write 1,200.00. My first parser stripped commas as
thousands separators, so 1200,00 became 120000 — a 100× error, silently, on every row.

The fix is not "be smarter about locales". It is a small decision tree where ambiguity loses:

if (/^\d{1,3}(\.\d{3})+(,\d+)?$/.test(s)) {
  s = s.replace(/\./g, "").replace(",", ".");        // 1.234,50 -> 1234.50
} else if (s.includes(",") && !s.includes(".")) {
  if (/^\d+,\d{2}$/.test(s)) s = s.replace(",", ".");          // 1200,00 -> 1200.00
  else if (/^\d{1,3}(,\d{3})+$/.test(s)) s = s.replace(/,/g, ""); // 1,200 -> 1200
  else return null;                                   // ambiguous: flag it, never guess
} else if (s.includes(",") && s.includes(".")) {
  if (/^\d{1,3}(,\d{3})+(\.\d+)?$/.test(s)) s = s.replace(/,/g, "");
  else return null;
}

return null means the cell is left exactly as typed and listed in a "needs a human eye" table.
On financial data, a wrong guess is worse than an unprocessed cell, because nobody notices it.

Bug 2: "fixed" dates that were still wrong

13/13/2026 should fail. Mine produced 2026-13-13 — a date that looks normalised, sorts
wrong, and breaks every downstream query. The validator needed to check the month, not only
whether the pattern matched:

const dmy = s.match(/^(\d{1,2})[.\/-](\d{1,2})[.\/-](\d{4})$/);
if (dmy && Number(dmy[1]) > 12 && Number(dmy[2]) <= 12) {
  return `${dmy[3]}-${dmy[2].padStart(2, "0")}-${dmy[1].padStart(2, "0")}`;
}

The tests that earned their keep

24 assertions, no framework — node test_cleaner.js, exit code 0 or it's broken. The three that
mattered most:

  • parseAmount("1200,00") === 1200 (not 120000)
  • parseDate("13/13/2026") === null (never a fake date)
  • cleaning must not change the sum of the amount column — that single assertion caught both bugs 
ok("sum of amounts unchanged by cleaning", () => {
  const sum = result.rows.filter((r) => /^-?\d+(\.\d+)?$/.test(r[2]))
    .reduce((a, r) => a + Number(r[2]), 0);
  assert.equal(Math.round(sum * 100) / 100, 1344.5);
});

If your cleaner can't state an invariant like that, you don't know what it did to the file.

What the tool does, and what it refuses to do

It trims cells, drops fully empty rows, drops exact duplicates (first occurrence wins),
normalises dates to YYYY-MM-DD when the meaning is unambiguous, and converts $1,234.50,
1.234,50 and (45.00) to plain decimals. Anything else is flagged.

It does not upload your file. There is no server: open the network tab and watch nothing
happen. That is also why it's free to run — the work is your browser's.

Try it: free CSV cleaner ·
proof run on a real 514-row sheet: csv-cleanup-proof

If a sheet is too far gone for a tool — merged header rows, amounts split across columns,
three date conventions in one file — that's what the done-for-you cleanup
is for: $49, one file, back within 24 hours with a page listing every change and every row I
refused to guess on.
